title: Joash: A Good Beginning and a Bitter End
summary: Joash, crowned at seven, does what is right as long as the priest Jehoiada lives, and he organizes a collection that restores the neglected temple. After Jehoiada dies, Joash listens to the officials of Judah, the nation turns to idols, and when Jehoiada's son Zechariah speaks God's warning, the king has him stoned in the temple court. An Aramean army humbles Judah, and Joash is murdered by his own servants and denied burial in the royal tombs.
story: The previous chapter told how Jehoiada the priest hid the boy Joash, the last surviving heir of David's line, and overthrew the usurping queen Athaliah. The promise to David had hung by the thread of one child. Now that child reigns for forty years, and the chapter splits his reign cleanly in two. In the first half he repairs the house of God; in the second he abandons it and kills the prophet God sends to call him back. The Chronicler is teaching his central lesson in miniature: seeking the LORD brings life, forsaking him brings ruin, and no good beginning guarantees a good end. The chapter also prepares for the reign of Amaziah, whose story follows the same pattern of a promising start and a later turn.
historical:
Joash (also spelled Jehoash) ruled Judah in the late ninth and early eighth centuries BC; common reconstructions place his reign at about 835 to 796 BC, though scholars' figures differ by a few years. The parallel account is 2 Kings 11:21 to 12:21. Kings tells of the collection chest and of an attack by Hazael, king of Aram, whose threat Joash bought off with temple and palace treasures (2 Kings 12:17-18). Chronicles adds material Kings does not have: Jehoiada's death at a great age, the officials' turn to idolatry, the prophetic warnings, and the stoning of Zechariah. It then reads the Aramean invasion and Joash's assassination as the consequence of that apostasy.

Aram, the kingdom centered on Damascus to the north, was the strongest local power in the region during these decades, and under Hazael it pressed hard on both Israel and Judah. The Chronicler's comment that the Arameans came "with only a few men" yet defeated "a very great army" (verse 24) reverses the pattern of earlier chapters, where a faithful Judah defeated larger forces.
cultural:
The temple's upkeep depended on offerings. The "tax imposed by Moses" (verse 6) refers to the half-shekel contribution for the tent of meeting described in Exodus 30:12-16, which the Chronicler presents as an annual obligation for temple service. Joash's chest at the gate made giving public and visible, and the joint emptying of it by the royal scribe and the high priest's officer (verse 11) was a simple safeguard against misuse. Kings adds that the chest had a hole bored in its lid and stood beside the altar (2 Kings 12:9).

Two details carry weight an ancient reader would feel at once. Burial with the kings in the City of David was an honor, and the Chronicler gives it to the priest Jehoiada (verse 16) while denying it to King Joash (verse 25). And bloodshed in the temple court was a desecration: the place where sacrifices made atonement became the place where an innocent man's blood was spilled. Zechariah's dying words ask God to see and to require an account, echoing the Old Testament conviction that innocent blood cries out to God (compare Genesis 4:10).
literary: The chapter is built as a diptych, two panels hinged on Jehoiada's death in verses 15-16. The first panel (verses 1-14) is about building up the house of the LORD; the second (verses 17-27) is about abandoning it. Key words link the halves. Joash "did what was right" in the days of Jehoiada (verse 2), but after Jehoiada the people "abandoned the house of the LORD" (verse 18). Zechariah's oracle turns on the same verb twice: "Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you" (verse 20), and the narrator repeats it in verse 24. The chapter also shows the Chronicler's habit of pairing guilt and consequence closely: the king who forgot the kindness of Jehoiada is killed "for shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest" (verse 25).

outline.t: The king orders the temple repaired
The collection chest and the restored house
Jehoiada dies and is buried with the kings
The officials lead Judah into idolatry

doctrines.note: The turn to Asherah poles and idols comes not through a foreign conqueror but through Judah's own officials, whom the king chooses to heed. Idolatry here is a slow drift under new influences once a faithful voice is gone.
God does not abandon Judah silently. He sends prophets, and the Spirit of God comes upon Zechariah to speak. The chapter shows that judgment follows only after warning has been given and refused.
The Chronicler draws a tight line between forsaking the LORD and being forsaken by him. Aram's small army defeating a great one shows that the outcome belongs to God, not to numbers.

words.note: Azav, to leave or forsake. It is the chapter's verdict word: the people abandoned the house of the LORD (verse 18), Zechariah announces that because they forsook him he has forsaken them (verse 20), and the narrator repeats it in verse 24. In Chronicles, forsaking is the opposite of seeking, the two paths every king chooses between.

Chesed, kindness or steadfast loyalty. It is often used of God's covenant love, but here it describes Jehoiada's faithful goodness to Joash, who owed the priest his life and his throne. Forgetting chesed is presented as a moral failure, not merely ingratitude.

Lavash, to clothe or put on. In verse 20 the Hebrew says the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah; the BSB renders it "came upon." The same striking image is used of Gideon (Judges 6:34) and Amasai (1 Chronicles 12:18): the Spirit takes hold of a person so that God speaks and acts through them.

Midrash, here translated "Treatise." In later Judaism the word came to mean interpretive commentary on Scripture, but in Chronicles (here and 13:22) it names one of the written sources the author consulted. What that work contained is not known.

christ: Jesus referred to this chapter when he warned the religious leaders of his day that the guilt of the righteous blood shed on earth would fall on their generation, "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" (Luke 11:51; compare Matthew 23:35). In the traditional order of the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles comes last, so Abel and Zechariah frame the whole of Scripture's record of murdered witnesses, from Genesis to Chronicles. Jesus placed himself at the end of that line, the prophet who would also be killed in Jerusalem. Yet where Zechariah prayed that the LORD would see and call his murderers to account, the letter to the Hebrews says that Jesus' sprinkled blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). The contrast is not in the text of Chronicles, but the New Testament draws it: the last innocent blood in this story brings forgiveness rather than a demand for vengeance.

hard.q: Matthew calls the murdered Zechariah the son of Berechiah, but this chapter says he was the son of Jehoiada. Which is it?
hard.a: Matthew 23:35 names Zechariah son of Berechiah, while 2 Chronicles 24:20 names Zechariah son of Jehoiada; Luke 11:51 gives no father's name. The prophet Zechariah of the late sixth century BC was the son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1), but the Old Testament does not record his death. Several explanations are offered. Some suggest that Jehoiada was Zechariah's grandfather or that Berechiah was a second name, since the word son can cover more distant descent. Others think a scribe or the Gospel tradition merged the two Zechariahs. Others argue Jesus meant a different, later Zechariah altogether, though the reference to the temple court and the Abel-to-Chronicles frame points strongly to this chapter. Most interpreters agree the murder in view is the one told here; how to account for the patronymic remains debated.

questions: Joash was faithful while Jehoiada lived and fell away soon after. Whose faith are you leaning on, and what would it take for it to become your own?
The officials who flattered the king led him away from God. What voices are you most inclined to listen to when a trusted guide is no longer present?
Joash forgot the kindness shown to him. How does remembering what others (and God) have done for you shape the way you treat their children, their causes, or their warnings?
